---
title: "Quiz: A difference between groups"
---

[Exercises](16-comparisons.qmd) · [Lecture slides](../lectures/16-comparisons/lec.qmd)

Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

---

**Q1.** Control mean growth is 15.28 mm and treated mean growth is 21.49 mm.
Calculate treated minus control from these rounded means. What does a
positive sign mean?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
State the subtraction order before calculating.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$21.49-15.28=6.21$ mm (about 6.22 mm from unrounded data). A positive
sign means greater mean growth in the treated sample.
:::

---

**Q2.** Twelve plants per treatment are measured initially and finally. How
many independent growth values are there per treatment: 12 or 24?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The two measurements belong to the same plant and yield one growth value.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**12**. Initial and final measurements are combined into one final-minus-initial
growth value per plant.
:::

---

**Q3.** Some control plants grew more than some treated plants. Does that force
the two sample means to be equal?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Individual overlap and equality of group means are different properties.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. Groups can overlap and still have different means. Use the observations
to describe overlap and calculate the group means separately.
:::

---

**Q4.** Which is the null hypothesis for the planned two-sided comparison?

(i) Every plant has identical growth.  

(ii) The two population mean growths are equal.  

(iii) The treatment must increase growth.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The hypothesis concerns population means, and a two-sided question allows
both directions of difference.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
(ii). The alternative allows either population mean to be larger. Individual
plants may vary under either hypothesis.
:::

---

**Q5.** The new class has a smaller sample mean difference than the first class.
Does the difference alone establish that the treatment stopped working? What
else do you need?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
An estimate varies across samples and conditions.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. Consider sampling uncertainty, observed variability, sample size, and
study conditions. A sample difference alone does not determine its uncertainty
or establish a universal treatment effect.
:::
